During Ramchandra Ray's escape, Sitaram is the submissive guard at the inner quarters door who obeys Udayaditya's command to open it, refuses to take up arms against him, and allows Udayaditya to disarm and bind him so Sitaram can shield him from the Maharaj, while Udayaditya leads the escape. On the night of Udayaditya's own escape from prison, the dynamic reverses: Sitaram becomes the active rescuer who throws open the prison door, grabs Udayaditya and almost carries him out, and directs him where to go, leaving Udayaditya as the dependent captive who asks Sitaram what to do and follows his lead.

Pratapaditya's initial plan was to send two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray while he took shelter at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; this failed because the Pathans refused to carry out the killing. The method that finally succeeded was a signed death sentence order delivered by Muktiyar Khan, which led an assassin named Abdul to enter Basanta Ray's room and kill him with a drawn sword.

Ramai Bhand faces physical retaliation from Rammohan Mal in two distinct instances: first, in the inner quarters of the palace while disguised as a woman (recognized as Ramai Thakur), where Rammohan seized, lifted, and tied him up with a shawl; and second, in the king's room while appearing in his normal role as the jester, where Rammohan grabbed him by the scruff of his neck and threw him out of the room.

The Rajmahishi secretly sent Matangini to fetch poison prepared by Mangala (Rukmini) through mantras and rituals; Surma consumed the poison and died, ending her stay in the palace rather than leaving for her father's house.

Ramchandra Ray regarded Vibha's refusal as a grave insult to his honor and took revenge by deciding to marry another woman. When Vibha finally arrived in Chandradwip, she discovered the King was getting married and had offered her no forgiveness, shattering all her hopes for happiness.

Rukmini obtained Udayaditya's ring, which bore a seal engraved with the Yubaraj's name, from him. Sitaram and Bhagavat used this ring to stamp a forged petition accusing the Yubaraj of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor in order to claim the kingdom for himself. Bhagavat then delivered the petition to Pratapaditya, claiming a servant of Udayaditya was taking it toward Delhi but had fled, leaving Bhagavat to bring it to the Maharaj. Upon seeing the petition bearing the Yubaraj's seal, Pratapaditya ordered Udayaditya imprisoned.

Ramchandra Ray's midnight escape leads to the dismissal of the palace guards, Sitaram and Bhagavat, who then fall into poverty. Udayaditya provides them with a monthly stipend, and Surma secretly sends the money to their families. When word of these secret stipends reaches Pratapaditya, he orders Surma to be sent to her paternal home.

The song expresses profound loneliness, emptiness, and grief, signifying that everything Basanta Ray once had is gone, only emptiness remains, and those who were once his no longer answer his call, leaving him to live with only himself. Basanta Ray sings it first while sitting alone on the veranda of his palace in Raigarh in the afternoon, gazing at the setting sun without his sitar, reflecting that there is no longer any joy in singing because those he sang for are no longer there. He sings it a second time in Vibha's room at the royal palace in Jessore, after learning of the Yubaraj's imprisonment, being refused help by Pratapaditya, and discovering that the room where joy once erupted is now silent, dark, and utterly empty.

Rukmini's failure to stop Udayaditya and Basanta Ray at the canal allowed them to flee to Raigarh. Because Basanta Ray sheltered the escaped Yubaraj there, Pratapaditya issued a secret death order against him through Muktiyar Khan. Muktiyar Khan carried out this order in Basanta Ray's room, and Basanta Ray accepted the execution rather than protecting Udayaditya, resulting in his death by sword.

Pratapaditya initially received Ramchandra Ray with cold indifference and a refusal to honor the occasion, claiming he did not know who should welcome his son-in-law, refusing to light the path or play music, and ignoring Ramchandra's presence to attend to court business such as a tax collector's complaint. In contrast, Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya's status in his own court with active verbal hostility and assertions of superiority; his minister and the jester Ramai Bhand publicly ridicule Pratapaditya's lineage, claiming his ancestors were earthworms and leeches and that his father required Ramchandra's grandfather to anoint him, while declaring that Chandradwip's marriage into Jessore redeemed seven generations of status. This marks a reversal of the perceived hierarchy, as Pratapaditya treated his son-in-law as an insignificant subordinate through neglect, whereas Ramchandra responded by systematically demeaning his father-in-law through daily public mockery to establish his own dominance.

The widow, Rukmini (who changed her name to Mangala), re-entered Jessore by living on its outskirts, befriending all the palace servants to track news, and presenting herself as a practitioner of tantra, mantra, and medicine. She caused tragedy by providing poison prepared over five days with mantras and rituals to the Rajmahishi, who intended to win the Yubaraj's heart back from Surma; Surma ultimately took the poison and died. Later, she physically re-entered Udayaditya's life by appearing in his room during a storm disguised as his deceased wife, Surma, manipulating his pity, taking his ring, and vowing to use her mantras against him.

Udayaditya's early lament about his unworthiness as crown prince culminates in a formal renunciation after his sister Vibha visits him in a panic, leading to his confrontation with his father Pratapaditya in Jessore. When brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner and told he is unworthy of the kingdom, Udayaditya confirms he does not want it and pleads for release from the throne. He then swears a solemn oath before the Ma-Kali temple that he will never rule even a needle's tip of Jessore's land, names Samaraditya as the heir, vows never to sit on the throne or touch the royal scepter, and departs for Kashi.

Nayanchand intercepted the letter when he reached Jessore; fearing what Pratapaditya might do if the letter fell into his hands, he resolved to give it to the Mahishi instead of delivering it to the Maharaj. Later, the Mahishi showed the letter to Basanta Ray, who misunderstood its intent as a sign of anger that would subside once Vibha was sent back, and advised her to announce that Ramchandra had written requesting Vibha be sent to Chandradwip. As a result, the Mahishi told Vibha and announced throughout the household that Ramchandra Ray had written a letter requesting that Vibha be sent to her in-laws' house, concealing the truth that he had actually written to renounce her and demand that she not be sent to Chandradwip again.

Pratapaditya ordered the canal adjoining the royal palace to be blocked immediately with large logs of Sal wood, where Ramchandra Ray’s boat was moored. However, when the boat reached the blockage, Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the logs. Additionally, when the guards tried to pursue by boat, the man sent to fetch the chase boat stopped at a shop to smoke tobacco and delayed to collect a debt, so the pursuing boat arrived long after Ramchandra Ray had escaped.

Basanta Ray abandons his beloved sitar at the moment he is separated from Udayaditya, telling him, “I am leaving this sitar behind, Dada, I will not play it anymore.” Before departing, his grief hinders his playing until his eyes blur with tears and his throat chokes, forcing him to put the sitar down. Later, he explains that although the sitar remains, “only its strings have broken, and it can no longer be tuned,” reflecting his own broken spirit and loss of joy in Udayaditya’s absence. This abandonment of his “eternal companion” marks the beginning of his despair, which deepens as he mourns the separation and culminates in complete devastation when the news of Udayaditya’s imprisonment arrives.

Earlier, Udayaditya was willing to involve himself in the affairs of his subjects and act against Pratapaditya's wishes, and he would previously have stopped officials from beating subjects without considering the consequences. After Surma's death, however, a strange, blind fear of Pratapaditya took hold of his mind and his former courage was gone. He hesitated in every task and doubt arose in every matter. Instead of intervening when an order was given to loot and burn the estate office of the zamindar of Chhapra, he told his servant to take the horse away. When he saw a subject being beaten, he ran into his house rather than protecting him as he would have before. Likewise, he no longer had the courage to send money to those in need, such as Bhagavat and Sitaram, hesitating until he never acted.

Sitaram undoes the damage by orchestrating the escape of the Yubaraj Udayaditya from the prison into which he had been confined. After consulting with Basanta Ray, Sitaram takes advantage of a fire that breaks out in the palace quarters; he enters Udayaditya's cell, tells him the prison is on fire, and carries him out to freedom.

On the first occasion, on the palace roof, Rammohan ties thick sheets together into a huge rope anchored to a pillar and climbs down it carrying Ramchandra Ray on his back; once at the end, he lowers the Maharaj carefully into the boat with his hands and jumps down himself. On the second occasion, after the king insults Vibha and she faints, Rammohan lifts her unconscious body, carries her out of the room, and places her into a waiting palanquin near the gate to take her to the boat.

In Jessore, the Mahishi adorns Vibha heavily with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm and a large nose ring, forcing a hairstyle she disliked, resulting in a regal presentation characterized by shy, joyous delight and "unruly glee." In Chandradwip, she instead dresses as a common woman and beggar-woman, refusing a palanquin by declaring, "Am I a queen that I should ask for a palanquin?", and enters the palace "like any other maidservant" with her veil pulled back over her head in shame, abandoning all royal splendor for humility and desperation.

In his bedchamber after Surma's death, the window serves as a place of longing and grief where Udayaditya sits waiting for Surma, expecting to see her or hear her voice amidst the familiar moonlight and garden, which ultimately highlights her absence. In the prison cell, however, the window becomes a symbol of freedom and hope; through the small opening, looking at the sky and flying birds allows Udayaditya to feel "naturally free" and imagine his chains breaking, whereas moving away from it leaves him seeing only darkness and the confinement of his prison.

Sitaram, a destitute guard, begins the arrangement by borrowing money from the wealthy widow Rukmini (Mangala) while masking his debt with flirtatious jokes and empty promises to repay, a dynamic Rukmini tolerates with feigned affection despite knowing that giving money to him offers less chance of recovery than throwing it in water. The relationship turns hostile when Sitaram, upon seeing the Yubaraj Udayaditya imprisoned, blames Rukmini and threatens to burn her house down and grind her face, provoking cold vengeance in her as she claims the Yubaraj is hers alone. Sitaram then aids Udayaditya's escape and stages his death by setting fire to the prison cell. Believing he must flee Jessore and needing money, Sitaram breaks into Rukmini's cottage at night. He finds her trembling in the dark, claiming she has 'returned from the door of Yama.' Instead of money, he encounters her intent on revenge; she vows to lay him and the Yubaraj in an oven to consecrate her body before Yama. When Sitaram feigns affection to defuse the tension, it enrages her further, and she retrieves a curved blade to attack him. Sitaram realizes his prior death jokes have become real threats and slips out of the cottage just as she strikes the floor where he stood, fleeing Jessore that very night. Rukmini then reports Sitaram's role in the escape and fire to the king before vanishing, ending their association in violence and betrayal.

Sitaram first ignites a fire in the guardhouse huts near the prison, creating a commotion that scatters the guards and leaves Udayaditya’s customary door guards unwatched. Seizing the distraction, he opens the prison door, tells Udayaditya the prison is on fire, and carries him out to escape on a boat. After Udayaditya reaches the river, Sitaram disembarks, returns to the city to recover Udayaditya’s letters, and shifts the strategy to a cover-up. He ensures the fire is not extinguished through sabotage by his men, then directs them to set fire to Udayaditya’s empty prison cell. Sitaram throws bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword into the room to fake his death, then spreads the news that the Yubaraj died when the roof collapsed. This false narrative is reinforced when witnesses claim to have seen or heard the Yubaraj and the melted remains of his sword are found by the king.

Ramchandra Ray shows no gratitude and dismisses Udayaditya's life-saving actions as insignificant, believing Udayaditya saved him primarily for the sake of his sister, Vibha, rather than for Ramchandra's own life, and considering the rescue merely inevitable. Instead of respecting his protective behavior, he laughs and jokes about Udayaditya in his own court alongside his courtiers, mocking him merely for being Pratapaditya’s son.

Pratapaditya initially dismisses the Emperor of Delhi's threat, telling his minister that the Emperor is "not my God" and forbidding him from mentioning Delhi while he orders the killing of his uncle. Later, the conspirators Sitaram and Bhagavat exploit this dismissed political fear by forging a petition bearing Prince Udayaditya's seal, presenting it as a complaint of treason from the Yubaraj against Pratapaditya submitted to the Emperor in order to seize the kingdom. Instead of sending the petition to Delhi, Bhagavat intercepts it and delivers it to Pratapaditya, claiming he found it after a servant of Udayaditya carrying it toward the Emperor had fled the country. This forged evidence leverages the Emperor's authority to incriminate the son, turning the threat Pratapaditya once scorned into the instrument used to convict him.

In the context of the Jessore palace, Vibha's hair grooming marks Surma's presence in Chapter 8, where Vibha, finding the Mahishi's styling unbearable, secretly goes to Surma to have her hair done to her own liking. Surma's subsequent tragic absence is marked by this same ritual in Chapter 18, where Vibha sits quietly when it is time to braid her hair, waiting for Surma to come at any moment, but evening falls and her hair remains unbraided. Later, in Chapter 23, Rammohan notes Vibha's hair is unkempt because there is no one left in the house to care for her, highlighting the void Surma's absence has left.
